checkpoints.prompt: Which deployment strategy sends only a small number of users to the new version first, instead of switching everyone at once?

choices.text: canary deployment
choices.explanation: A canary deployment observes the new version with a portion of the traffic before expanding its reach.

choices.text: Rolling out all users in stages only
choices.explanation: This does not describe limiting the rollout to a small number of users; it refers broadly to staged update strategies.

choices.text: Big bang in a single environment
choices.explanation: A big bang switches everyone at once, so it does not narrow the impact scope first.

choices.text: database backup
choices.explanation: A backup is a recovery method, not a deployment strategy.

checkpoints.title: Control the impact scope with deployment strategies

checkpoints.prompt: The canary error rate exceeds the baseline, and abort criteria were defined in advance. What should you do next?

choices.text: Record that the criteria were exceeded, stop the rollout from expanding, and proceed to investigate or recover.
choices.explanation: Predefined abort criteria are used to control the impact instead of continuing to expand based on intuition.

choices.text: Increase traffic to 100% and dilute the error rate by averaging.
choices.explanation: Expanding while the criteria are exceeded widens the impact.

choices.text: Rewrite the baseline with the new version’s values.
choices.explanation: Changing the baseline to hide an anomaly undermines the basis for observation.

choices.text: Continue based only on the scheduled time without measuring the error rate.
choices.explanation: Staged rollouts are guided by observed values and abort criteria.

checkpoints.title: Observe and apply the abort criteria

checkpoints.prompt: The new code has started writing to the old DB schema, and the data format can no longer be read after reverting to the old version. Which recovery decision should you make first?

choices.text: Check DB compatibility and the data recovery point, not just code rollback.
choices.explanation: Reverting the code does not restore data that has already changed, so decide how to recover based on the DB state as well.

choices.text: Deleting the new artifact will also return the DB to its old format.
choices.explanation: Deleting the artifact does not reverse data transformations.

choices.text: Directly delete the DB without checking whether a backup exists.
choices.explanation: Direct deletion increases data loss and destroys recovery points.

choices.text: Assume the incident is resolved if you stop monitoring.
choices.explanation: Stopping observation is not recovery; it only hides the impact.

checkpoints.title: Choose rollback or roll forward

checkpoints.prompt: For database changes made while old and new application versions are running simultaneously, select two steps that improve safety.

choices.text: First perform an expand step, such as adding a backward-compatible column.
choices.explanation: Performing compatible changes that keep the old version running first preserves reads and writes during a gradual rollout.

choices.text: Restore to an isolated environment, then verify the recovered contents and the time required.
choices.explanation: This lets you confirm that the backup can actually be restored without disrupting production.

choices.text: Deploy only the new code first, then immediately stop the old version.
choices.explanation: Switching over without checking compatibility during simultaneous operation leaves fewer recovery options.

choices.text: Remove schema changes from the history to make rollback easier.
choices.explanation: Deleting history does not restore actual data and also loses traceability.

checkpoints.title: Design database compatibility and recovery

choices.text: Canary sends a small amount of traffic to the new version, then expands the rollout after observing the results.
choices.explanation: Canary exposes the new version to users gradually.

choices.text: Blue/green deletes the old environment before creating the new one.
choices.explanation: This approach validates the old and new environments side by side, then shifts traffic.

choices.text: Rolling switches all traffic to the new environment at once.
choices.explanation: Rolling replaces instances or tasks a few at a time.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one correct description of rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments.
finalQuestions.title: Deployment strategies

choices.text: If you can provision duplicate resources and validate before switching over, consider blue/green deployment.
choices.explanation: You can validate the old and new environments side by side.

choices.text: If you want to assess the impact using a small amount of real traffic, consider a canary deployment.
choices.explanation: You can check the impact in production while limiting the blast radius.

choices.text: With a rolling deployment, there is no period when the old and new versions run at the same time.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The versions are replaced incrementally, so there is a period when the old and new versions coexist.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one incorrect statement about deployment strategies.
finalQuestions.title: Choosing a strategy

choices.text: If avoiding downtime is important and the cost of running two environments is acceptable, consider blue/green.
choices.explanation: This takes into account pre-cutover testing and the cost of keeping the old environment running.

choices.text: Deploy based on the strategy name alone, without deciding on database compatibility or traffic shifting.
choices.explanation: Coexistence requirements and data state also need to be designed.

choices.text: Monitoring is unnecessary with canary because only a small number of users see it.
choices.explanation: Even with a small audience, monitor the impact on live traffic.

choices.text: For canary deployments that start with limited impact, define the stages, waiting periods, and stop conditions.
choices.explanation: This makes decisions about expanding the rollout reproducible.

choices.text: With rolling deployments, you do not need to consider the remaining capacity.
choices.explanation: Check capacity and availability during replacement.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two correct judgments when selecting a strategy.
finalQuestions.title: Comparing strategies

choices.text: Stop the rollout if a predefined error rate or latency threshold is exceeded.
choices.explanation: Stop based on quantified criteria.

choices.text: If CPU is normal, do not check the error rate.
choices.explanation: Monitor user impact beyond CPU as well.

choices.text: If observability is unavailable, stop expanding traffic, save the logs, and move on to investigating the cause.
choices.explanation: Do not treat an unobservable state as normal; stop the expansion and preserve evidence.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two correct actions for deciding whether to abort during a rollout.
finalQuestions.title: Abort criteria

choices.text: Compare the error rate, latency, and business success rate of the old and new versions.
choices.explanation: Check the impact of the change using multiple metrics.

choices.text: Increase traffic after assuming there is no problem, even if some monitoring is missing.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. If you cannot observe the system, do not increase traffic; improve the measurements first.

choices.text: Continue even after a threshold is exceeded, without saving the deployment ID and logs.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Stop, save the evidence, and use it to investigate the cause.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two actions that are incorrect when responding to a canary deployment.
finalQuestions.title: Observability

choices.text: Decide in advance on the thresholds, wait times, and the action for restoring traffic.
choices.explanation: This makes decisions and actions reproducible.

choices.text: Continue if the CPU is normal, even when the business success rate worsens.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Worsening business metrics are also a reason to stop.

choices.text: When a threshold is exceeded, do not proceed to the next stage; save the logs.
choices.explanation: This limits the impact and preserves evidence.

choices.text: Compare the old and new versions’ metrics under the same conditions.
choices.explanation: You can assess the impact of the change from the differences.

choices.text: Expand the rollout, treating metrics that cannot be measured as normal.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. You cannot make a safe decision when observability is unavailable.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the two incorrect statements about monitoring and abort criteria.
finalQuestions.title: A combination that should trigger an abort

choices.text: Rollback returns to a known-good version, while rollforward advances with a corrected version as a new revision.
choices.explanation: The two differ in the direction and target of recovery.

choices.text: Rollback also automatically reverts the database state to an earlier point.
choices.explanation: Code and data recovery must be designed separately.

choices.text: A CodeDeploy rollback only restores a past deployment in time.
choices.explanation: It redistributes an earlier revision as a new deployment.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one correct statement about rollback and rollforward.
finalQuestions.title: Rollback

choices.text: First, limit the impact by routing traffic back to the previous version or stopping the deployment.
choices.explanation: This reduces the scope of impact while the cause is being investigated.

choices.text: Check the cause, then decide whether to proceed with a fix or return to a healthy revision.
choices.explanation: Choose between rollforward and rollback based on the situation.

choices.text: Treat recovery as complete as soon as you have performed a rollback once, without confirming that recovery succeeded.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Verify health, business outcomes, and data integrity.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the one incorrect statement about recovery procedures during an incident.
finalQuestions.title: Recovery procedures

choices.text: Return traffic to a known-good revision to stop the impact quickly.
choices.explanation: This is a basic way to limit impact with a rollback.

choices.text: Reverting the code will always restore destroyed data.
choices.explanation: Data requires a separate recovery procedure.

choices.text: Remove the threshold and send all traffic again, even if the cause is unknown.
choices.explanation: Do not expand the impact without checking the cause and the criteria.

choices.text: Choose a rollforward if the cause is known and the fix can be tested safely.
choices.explanation: This means proceeding with the fix as a new revision.

choices.text: There is no need to check the business success rate after recovery.
choices.explanation: Check both the technical state and the business outcome.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two correct statements about when to use rollback and rollforward.
finalQuestions.title: Recovery strategy

choices.text: Separate adding, switching code, and removing the old format, and allow a period when the old and new versions can coexist.
choices.explanation: This lets the old version in the rolling deployment handle the new schema.

choices.text: Remove the columns used by the old version immediately after adding the new columns.
choices.explanation: This is a breaking change that will prevent the old version from running.

choices.text: Because a backup exists, there is no need to rehearse a restore.
choices.explanation: Restore capability and data consistency must be verified in practice.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct approach for a deployment that involves a database change.
finalQuestions.title: Database Compatibility

choices.text: After restoring from a snapshot, verify consistency and that the application can reconnect.
choices.explanation: Verify availability, not just that the restore operation completed.

choices.text: Even after a destructive migration, a code rollback alone restores the previous data.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The code and database state are separate, so restoring from a backup or similar is necessary.

choices.text: Include recovery time and acceptable data loss in the plan.
choices.explanation: Reflect RTO/RPO in the recovery design.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about database recovery.
finalQuestions.title: Data recovery

choices.text: Add the schema first in a form the old version can ignore.
choices.explanation: This is a phased change that lets the old and new versions coexist.

choices.text: Immediately change to a column the old version cannot read, even during a rolling deployment.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It breaks compatibility with the old version.

choices.text: After restoring a backup, check consistency, differences, and reconnection.
choices.explanation: This verifies availability after restoration.

choices.text: Perform an irreversible transformation only after preparing a snapshot and recovery procedure.
choices.explanation: This ensures in advance that there is a way to restore the data state.

choices.text: Assume that a code rollback will also restore data deleted from the DB.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Data requires a separate restore or compensating operation.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two incorrect statements about DB compatibility and recovery.
finalQuestions.title: Safe DB Deployment

blocks.label: Control the blast radius with deployment strategies
blocks.text: A rolling deployment replaces running instances with the new version a few at a time. You can update without stopping everything, but you need to account for the period when both versions are running and for the remaining capacity.

blocks.label: Control the blast radius with deployment strategies
blocks.text: A blue/green deployment runs the old blue and new green environments side by side, validates them, and switches traffic. You can check green before the switch and return to blue more easily if problems occur, but this requires double the resources.

blocks.label: Control the blast radius with deployment strategies
blocks.text: A canary deployment initially sends only a small amount of traffic to the new version, then expands the scope after observing the results. You can validate it with real traffic, but you need to decide how to select targets, the rollout stages, the wait time, and the stop conditions.

steps.label: Control the blast radius with deployment strategies

blocks.label: Control the blast radius with deployment strategies
blocks.text: Choose a strategy based on acceptable downtime, additional cost, the blast radius of the change, and rollback speed. Don’t assume a strategy is safe based on its name alone; also check the conditions for running the old and new versions side by side.

blocks.label: Observe and Apply Abort Criteria
blocks.text: During deployment, compare the old and new versions in terms of error rate, latency, traffic, and saturation. Also check whether errors have increased in users’ critical operations.

blocks.label: Set abort criteria in advance using measurable thresholds—for example, the error rate exceeds the acceptable limit, p95 latency exceeds the predefined value, or a health check fails. A vague instruction such as “stop if there’s a problem” delays the decision.
blocks.text: For canary or blue/green deployments, decide how long to wait for observations and how to shift traffic back. If a threshold is exceeded, do not proceed to the next stage; save the evidence and begin investigating the cause.

blocks.label: Observe and Apply Abort Criteria
blocks.text: Observe and Apply Abort Criteria

blocks.label: Observe and apply stop criteria
blocks.text: Even when monitoring looks healthy, business errors that aren't measured can go unnoticed. Combine technical metrics with important business outcomes, and do not expand the rollout when the state cannot be observed.

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: During the canary, the new version’s p95 latency exceeded the threshold.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Compare the latency, error rate, and business success rate of the old and new versions.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the predefined abort threshold.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Stop the traffic increase, roll back to the previous version, and save the logs and deployment ID.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Stop based on observed data rather than intuition, so you can investigate the cause later.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If CPU is healthy, there is no user impact, so it is fine to continue the deployment.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Check indicators that reflect the impact of the change, such as errors, latency, and business success rate, not just CPU.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Define the metrics to monitor and the abort thresholds in advance.

blocks.label: If a threshold is exceeded, stop the rollout and, if necessary, shift traffic back.
blocks.text: Combine technical and business metrics.

blocks.text: AWS CodeDeploy deployment monitoring.

blocks.label: Choose between rollback and rollforward
blocks.text: Rollback means returning to a known-good version. In CodeDeploy, a rollback redistributes a previous revision as a new deployment, so it is not simply an operation that turns back time.

blocks.label: Rollforward is a way to move forward with a new revision that fixes the problem. Choose it when the cause is in the configuration or code and you can safely validate the corrected version in a short time.
blocks.text: First, take steps to limit the impact, such as routing traffic back to the old version, stopping the deployment, or turning off the feature flag. Then investigate the cause and determine the scope of recovery.

blocks.label: Choosing rollback or rollforward
blocks.text: Rollback does not always succeed. Rehearse compatibility between the old and new versions, external dependencies, changed data, and the permissions required for the procedure in advance; decide on the recovery time and who will make the decision.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can first stop the impact, then choose a recovery method without confusing it with the cause.

blocks.label: Design database compatibility and recovery
blocks.text: When old and new versions of an application run at the same time during a deployment, you need to preserve data formats and APIs that both versions can read. Add columns in a way that the old version can ignore, and schedule deletions or changes in meaning for a time when the old version is no longer running.

blocks.label: Design database compatibility and recovery
blocks.text: A safe change follows a gradual process: first add compatible columns or tables, then switch the code to the new format, and remove the old format only after no code uses it.

blocks.label: Creating a backup does not mean recovery is complete. Test the restore procedure, restore destination, RPO/RTO, consistency checks, and application reconnection in practice.
blocks.text: Design database compatibility and recovery

blocks.label: Design database compatibility and recovery
blocks.text: Rolling back only the code after data loss or an irreversible transformation will not restore historical data. Include measures such as making migrations reversible, retaining snapshots, and handling changes made after recovery in the change plan.

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: Add a new shipping category to orders and perform a rolling deployment.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: First, add a nullable column that the old version can ignore.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Deploy the code with a period during which both the old and new versions can read it.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After the old version is no longer needed, remove constraints or obsolete columns in a separate change.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can avoid format mismatches while old and new versions run side by side, and restore the code and database together.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Because a snapshot exists, a code rollback alone will restore the original state even after a destructive migration.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Restoration from a snapshot and checks for data loss and differences are required. Changing the code version alone does not restore the database state.

blocks.label: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Design schemas and APIs that allow old and new versions to coexist.

blocks.label: Separate additions, switches, and removals, and defer breaking changes until later.
blocks.text: For backups, perform restoration drills and verify consistency.
